Surah al-Humazah is Meccan [Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "(Woe to every backbiter and slanderer) was revealed in Makkah." See al-Durr al-Manthur: 8/623.] In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

* *

﴿Woe to every backbiter and slanderer.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: They are those who go about spreading gossip (namimah), who separate loved ones, and who seek out the faults of the innocent. [Narrated by Sa'id ibn Mansur. See: Fath al-Bari 8/729.] Both words have the same meaning, which is one who finds fault constantly.

Muqatil said: "al-Humazah" is one who finds fault with you in your absence, and "al-Lumazah" is one who finds fault with you to your face. Abu al-'Aliyah and al-Hasan said the opposite of this.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Qatadah said: "al-Humazah" is one who eats the flesh of people by backbiting them, and "al-Lumazah" is one who attacks them with insults.

Ibn Zayd said: "al-Humazah" is one who strikes people with his hand and beats them, and "al-Lumazah" is one who defames them with his tongue and disparages them.

Sufyan al-Thawri said: he strikes with his tongue and defames with his eye. Ibn Kaysan said likewise: "al-Humazah" is one who harms his companion with bad speech, and "al-Lumazah" is one who winks with his eye, gestures with his head, and signals with his eyebrow, and both are intensive adjectives for the doer, like sukhrah and dahkah: for one who mocks and laughs at people. [Al-Humzah and al-Lumzah, with the mim unvocalised (sakinah), refer to the one to whom such things are done.]

The root meaning of hamz is to crush and to bite down on something forcefully.

They differed about who this verse was revealed concerning. Al-Kalbi said: it was revealed concerning al-Akhnas ibn Shariq ibn Wahb al-Thaqafi, who used to attack people and backbite them. [Attributed by al-Suyuti in al-Durr al-Manthur 8/623 to Ibn Abi Hatim from al-Suddi.]

Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: "We have always heard that Surah al-Humazah [was revealed concerning Umayyah ibn Khalaf al-Jumahi]." [The words in brackets are missing from manuscript "A"; see Ibn Hisham 1/382.]

Muqatil said: it was revealed concerning al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, who used to backbite the Prophet (ﷺ) behind his back and revile him to his face.

Mujahid said: it is general in application to everyone who has this description.

Then He described him, saying: ﴿Who has gathered wealth﴾. Abu Ja'far, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "jamma'a" with the letter mim doubled (shaddah), indicating intensification. The others read it with the mim unstressed.

﴿And counts it﴾: he counted it, that is, he kept an account of it. Muqatil said: he prepared it, stored it up, and made it a provision for himself. It is said: a'addtu [al-shay'] [[Omitted from manuscript "A".]] and 'addadtuhu, meaning, I held onto it.

﴿He thinks his wealth will make him immortal﴾: in this world; he thinks that he will not die because of his affluence.

﴿No!﴾: a rebuke to him, that his wealth will not make him immortal. ﴿He will surely be thrown﴾: he will surely be cast out, ﴿into the Crusher﴾: into Hell. Al-Hutamah is one of the names of the Fire, like Saqar and Laza [[This is the view of al-Farra', and al-Bukhari mentioned it in his chapter heading: 8/729.]]. It was named "Hutamah" because it crushes and breaks the bones.

﴿And what will make you know what the Crusher is? It is the Fire of Allah, kindled, which mounts over the hearts﴾: that is, its pain and agony reach the hearts. Al-ittila' (mounting) and al-bulugh (reaching) have one meaning. It is related from the Arabs: "When did you reach (tala'ta) our land?", meaning, when did you arrive.

The meaning of the verse: it consumes everything of him until it reaches his heart. This was said by al-Qurazi and al-Kalbi.

Commentary of al-Baghawi (Ma'alim al-Tanzil) on surah 104, verses 8–9:

﴿Indeed, it will be closed over them﴾, meaning sealed shut and locked.

﴿In extended columns﴾. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr recited ﴿fi ʿumudin﴾ with a ḍammah on the ʿayn and the mīm, while the others recited it with a fatḥah on both, as in His saying: "He raised the heavens without pillars that you can see" [al-Ra'd: 2]. Both forms are the plural of ʿamūd (pillar), like adīm (hide) and adam, and udum [[Omitted from "B".]]. This was said by al-Farra' [[See: Ma'ani al-Qur'an by al-Farra': 3/291.]].

Abu ʿUbaydah said: it is the plural of ʿimād (pole), like ihāb (hide) and ahab and uhub [[al-Fayyumi said in "al-Misbah al-Munir" 1/28: "al-Ihab: the hide... Its plural is ahab", with two ḍammahs according to analogy, like kitab and kutub, and with two fatḥahs contrary to analogy. Some have said: in the speech of the Arabs there is no fa'al pattern plural of the form fa'l with two fatḥahs except ihab and ahab, and ʿimad and ʿamad.]].

Ibn ʿAbbas said: "He will place them in columns, and they will be stretched over them with poles."

[It was said: "in extended columns" refers to] the iron chains around their necks.

[It was said: "They are extended columns": at the gate of Hell,] by which the gates are sealed over them, so that they cannot get out.

Qatadah said: "We have been told that they are columns with which they will be tortured in the Fire."

It was also said: they are the stakes of the enclosures that close over the people of the Fire, meaning that they are closed over them with extended stakes. In the recitation of ʿAbdullah it is "bi-ʿumudin" with a bāʾ.

Muqatil said: the gates close over them, then they are secured with iron stakes of fire, so that their grief and heat return upon them; no gate is opened for them and no relief enters upon them. The word "extended" (mumaddadah) is an attribute of the columns, meaning elongated, so that they are firmer than short ones.
